summary: This informational memo describes version 2 of the Internet Cache Protocol as implemented in two web proxy cache packages, which lets caches ask their neighbors whether they hold a copy of an object.

eli5.summary: Neighboring libraries ask one another if they have a book before ordering it.

questions: what is the internet cache protocol
subtitle: A lightweight message format that lets web caches ask their neighbors whether they already hold a URL.

tldr.problem: A web cache that misses on an object needs to find out quickly which neighbor cache has it, without the overhead of setting up a TCP connection to each one.
tldr.mechanism: ICP defines a 20-octet fixed header plus a payload. A cache sends a query naming a URL, and each neighbor answers with a HIT, a MISS or another reply code, usually over UDP.
tldr.outcome: This informational memo records how ICP version 2 was already implemented in two web proxy cache packages. It describes only message formats and fields; a companion document, RFC 2187, covers how caches apply it.

today: RFC 2186 is an Informational memo and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It documents existing practice rather than setting a standard, and it leaves the application of ICP to its companion, RFC 2187.

sections.title: Why Caches Need a Lighter Protocol
sections.content:
The Internet Cache Protocol (ICP) is a message format that web caches use to talk to each other. Caches still move the actual object data with HTTP, but they benefit from something simpler and lighter for finding it. In a cache mesh, one cache sends an ICP query to its neighbors, and the neighbors reply with a HIT or a MISS.

In current practice ICP runs on top of UDP, although the RFC says nothing requires that. The reasoning is about timing. A query and reply need to happen within a second or two, because a cache cannot wait longer before it starts fetching the object. A missing reply most likely means the network path is congested or broken, and the cache would not want to pick that neighbor anyway. UDP's lack of overhead makes it a good probe of immediate network conditions.

ICP started with Peter Danzig and colleagues at the University of Southern California, as a central part of hierarchical caching in the Harvest research project. The memo covers only the format and fields of the messages. Version two was in use in two web proxy cache packages, and the authors wanted to codify existing practice.
sections.eli5: Before fetching a web page the slow way, a cache quickly asks its friends if they already have it. A short note works better than a long conversation, and if a friend does not answer in a second or two, the cache just skips them.

sections.title: The ICP Message Format
sections.content:
Every ICP message has a fixed header of 20 octets followed by a variable-size payload. All fields are in network byte order, and a message must not exceed 16,384 octets.

  • Opcode and Version: the message type, and the protocol version. Versions two and three were both in use when the memo was written; this document describes only version two.
  • Message Length: the total length of the message in octets.
  • Request Number: an opaque identifier that must be copied into the reply to a query.
  • Options: 32 bits of flags that allow limited extension of the protocol.
  • Option Data: a four-octet field for optional features. The round-trip-time option uses its low 16 bits.
  • Sender Host Address: the IPv4 address of the sender. The RFC warns it should probably not be trusted over what the socket calls report, and says that in practice it is not used.

The payload depends on the opcode. Most often it is a null-terminated URL string.
sections.eli5: Every ICP note starts with the same short label that says what kind of note it is, how long it is, and which question it answers. The rest of the note, usually a web address, comes after the label.

sections.title: Queries and Replies
sections.content:
A cache sends ICP_OP_QUERY with the URL it wants. The payload starts with a Requester Host Address, which is the address of the cache's client rather than the cache itself and is often zero filled, meaning not specified. The recipient must answer with one of six replies, copying the URL and the Request Number exactly.

  • ICP_OP_HIT: the URL is in this cache and the requester is allowed to retrieve it.
  • ICP_OP_MISS: the URL is not in this cache. The querying cache may still choose to fetch it from the replying cache.
  • ICP_OP_ERR: an error in parsing or handling the query, such as an invalid URL.
  • ICP_OP_MISS_NOFETCH: the cache is up but does not want to handle misses right now, for example while rebuilding its object store. It is a request to not fetch the URL from it.
  • ICP_OP_DENIED: the querying site is not allowed to retrieve the object. A cache getting a high share of these is probably misconfigured; the RFC gives 95% of 100 or more queries as an example threshold for disabling a neighbor.
  • ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ: a hit with the object data included in the reply.

ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ is NOT recommended. It bypasses normal HTTP processing, including authorization and age validation, and its messages are often much larger than the path MTU, causing UDP fragmentation. A cache must not send it unless the query set the ICP_FLAG_HIT_OBJ flag.

Two further opcodes let a cache include servers that do not speak ICP in its closest-neighbor selection. ICP_OP_SECHO bounces a message off an origin server's echo port, and ICP_OP_DECHO does the same to a cache that does not use ICP. Messages with unrecognized or unused opcodes should be ignored with no reply, though they may be logged.
sections.eli5: You ask a neighbor, do you have this one? They can say yes, no, there was a mix-up, I am busy so please do not ask me to fetch it, or you are not allowed to have it. They can even hand you the page right away, but that is not a great idea.

sections.title: Option Flags
sections.content:
Two option flags are defined in the Options field. ICP_FLAG_HIT_OBJ (0x80000000) is set in a query to say it is okay to answer with ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ if the object fits in the reply.

ICP_FLAG_SRC_RTT (0x40000000) asks the responder to include its measured round-trip time to the origin server named in the URL. When the value is available, it MUST be a 16-bit integer in milliseconds, carried in the low 16 bits of Option Data. If it is not available, the responder may set the value to zero or clear the flag in the reply. The reply MUST NOT be delayed while waiting for a measurement. If the flag is clear in the query it MUST be clear in the reply; if it is set in the query, it may or may not be set in the reply.
sections.eli5: A question can come with extra requests. One says it is fine to send the whole page back, and the other asks how long it takes you to reach the original web site. You can answer quickly without the extra if you do not know.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This memo does not discuss security itself. It says the security issues relating to ICP are covered in the companion document, RFC 2187. Within this document, the only security-relevant advice is narrow: do not trust the Sender Host Address field over what the operating system reports about the packet, and be cautious with ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ, which skips HTTP authorization checks.
sections.eli5: The note about security is in a different document. This one only warns that you should not believe the return address written on the note, and that handing over a page directly skips the usual checks.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: ICP version number; this document describes version two.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message in octets, at most 16,384.

fields.name: Request Number
fields.desc: Opaque identifier copied into the reply.

fields.name: Option Data
fields.desc: Four octets for optional features, such as the RTT value.

fields.name: Sender Host Address
fields.desc: IPv4 address of the sender; in practice not used.

items.label: ICP_OP_INVALID
items.desc: Placeholder to detect zero-filled or malformed messages; never sent on purpose.

items.label: ICP_OP_QUERY
items.desc: Asks whether a URL is held.

items.label: ICP_OP_HIT
items.desc: The URL is in this cache and may be retrieved.

items.label: ICP_OP_MISS
items.desc: The URL is not in this cache.

items.label: ICP_OP_ERR
items.desc: Error parsing or handling the query.

items.label: ICP_OP_SECHO
items.desc: Simulated query to an origin server's echo port.

items.label: ICP_OP_DECHO
items.desc: Simulated query to a cache that does not use ICP.

items.label: ICP_OP_MISS_NOFETCH
items.desc: Up, but please do not fetch this URL from me now.

items.label: ICP_OP_DENIED
items.desc: The querying site may not retrieve this object.

items.label: ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ
items.desc: A hit with the object data included; not recommended.
